q: Filling a flute in two stages rather than one achieves what?
opts: The wine is held closer to its serving temperature
The wine picks up useful oxygen between the two pours
The first foam subsides so a full measure fits in the glass
Pressure in the bottle is reduced for the next pour
exp: A single pour into a cold, narrow glass is almost all head and goes over the lip before the measure is in. A small pour, a pause, then the rest, and the glass ends correctly filled to about two thirds.

q: Tilting the glass and pouring down its inner wall does what for a sparkling wine?
exp: Bubbles break where wine strikes a flat surface hard. Down the side, more gas stays in solution and the wine keeps its texture as well as its look.

q: An unfinished bottle of Champagne has to hold its pressure overnight. Which closure does that job?
exp: A sprung clamp grips the lip of the bottle and holds several atmospheres. The teaspoon in the neck is folklore and does nothing whatever.

q: A bottle has lain on its side for thirty years and is on tonight's order. What should have been done to it yesterday?
accept: stood upright a day before service
ans: Stood upright a day before service
exp: Sediment lying along the flank of a bottle cannot be decanted cleanly. A day standing pulls it into the punt, where a careful pour can leave it behind.

q: Two decants, a young Barolo and a 1971 Burgundy, differ in handling how?
opts: The old wine is poured hard for air and the young one poured gently
Neither is poured until the wine has reached room temperature
Both are poured hard and rested for an hour before service
The young wine is aired and the old one poured off its deposit
exp: One decant is for air and the other is for sediment, and they call for opposite handling: the Barolo is poured hard and left to open, the Burgundy poured gently and served straight away. A fragile old wine can fall apart in the decanter within twenty minutes.

q: A light is set under the neck of the bottle during a decant. What is the server watching for?
exp: A candle is traditional and a phone torch does the same work. The pour stops the moment the cloud arrives at the shoulder, and the last inch stays behind.

q: A fifteen-year-old Rioja Gran Reserva is ordered and the table asks whether it wants a decanter. Which reply is soundest?
opts: Never decant Spanish wine, since it has already had long cask ageing
Taste it first and decant if it is closed or throwing sediment
Decant anything older than ten years as a matter of house policy
Decant only when a guest specifically asks for it
exp: Age alone settles nothing. Gran Reserva has usually spent years in cask and may be perfectly open already, in which case air costs it more than it gives. Deposit is the separate question, and a bottle at fifteen years that is dropping any goes into a decanter whether it needs air or not.

q: Bottled unfiltered and throwing a heavy crust, which fortified wine is decanted as a matter of routine?
exp: The crust forms because the wine goes into bottle young and unfiltered. Tawny, aged in cask and filtered before bottling, needs nothing of the kind.

q: Which piece of equipment sits in the neck of the decanter to catch cork fragments and coarse deposit?
exp: The better ones carry an angled spout that runs wine down the wall of the decanter rather than dropping it into the middle, which suits a fragile old red.

q: Ice alone chills a bottle slowly and unevenly. What else goes into the bucket?
exp: Air between cubes insulates, so dry ice cubes touch only a fraction of the glass. Half ice and half water chills several times faster.

q: The red has stood by the pass all evening and now tastes hot and blurred. What is the remedy?
opts: An ice cube dropped into each glass
A hard decant to drive off some of the alcohol
A few minutes in ice to bring it toward sixteen degrees
A second bottle opened and blended with the first
exp: Above about eighteen degrees alcohol dominates and definition disappears. Five minutes in a bucket rescues a wine that had seemed faulty.

q: Serving a fine white straight out of a full ice bucket costs the guest what?
opts: Its colour, which fades at low temperature
Most of its aroma and much of its texture
Its alcohol, which evaporates in the bucket
Its acidity, which cold strips away
exp: Aromatic compounds need warmth to volatilise, so a serious white shows least at four degrees. A bucket is for holding a temperature, not for reaching one.

q: Cold hardens one structural component of a red and mutes the aromatics. Which component turns harsher?
exp: The same bottle at ten degrees and at sixteen can seem to be two wines. An over-chilled red reads as tough and bitter when nothing at all is wrong with it.

q: Which two Sherry styles are served as cold as a white wine and treated as perishable once opened?
exp: Both age under flor and are bottled at modest strength, so they oxidise much as a table wine does. A bottle open for a week has nothing left worth selling.

q: A restaurant with no cellar keeps its reds in a kitchen at twenty-two degrees. Which single purchase most improves service?
exp: Wine stored warm is tired before it is opened, and no amount of ice at the table undoes that. Storage decides more about a bottle than service ever can.

q: Bottle after bottle of one producer's screwcapped white smells dank and musty, and fresh glasses change nothing. Which source does that pattern implicate?
exp: Musty taint compounds form from chlorophenols in cellar timber, cartons and cleaning products, then drift through a building and are taken up by the wine long before bottling. A screwcap closes the closure route and nothing else. Odd single bottles across many wines suggest closures, while a whole run from one address suggests the address.
